UNIT III: DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING
Dynamic Programming (DP) is an algorithmic technique that solves complex problems by breaking
them into overlapping subproblems, storing results to avoid recomputation — a process called
memoization or tabulation.
3.1 The General Method
Dynamic Programming is applicable when a problem has:
• Optimal Substructure: Optimal solution of a problem contains optimal solutions to
subproblems.
• Overlapping Subproblems: Same subproblems are solved repeatedly.
Two Approaches

Two Approaches
Top-Down (Memoization) 	Bottom-Up (Tabulation)
Recursive + cache results 	Iterative, fill table from base cases
Easier to implement 	More efficient (no recursion overhead)
Uses call stack 	Uses array/table
Computes only needed subproblems 	Computes all subproblems
General DP Steps
1. Characterize the structure of an optimal solution.
2. Recursively define the value of an optimal solution.
3. Compute the value bottom-up (or top-down with memoization).

4. Reconstruct the optimal solution from computed information.
Key Formula: DP[i] = optimal(DP[i-1], DP[i-2], ...) — each state builds on previously solved
states.

3.2 Bellman-Ford Algorithm
Finds shortest paths from a single source to all vertices in a weighted directed graph. Unlike Dijkstra, it
handles negative edge weights.
Core Concept
• Relaxation: If dist[v] > dist[u] + w(u,v), update dist[v].
• Perform relaxation (V-1) times for all edges.
• Detect negative-weight cycles in the Vth pass.
Algorithm
BellmanFord(G, src):
Initialize dist[] = ∞ for all vertices; dist[src] = 0
Repeat (V-1) times:
For each edge (u, v, w):
if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:

if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
dist[v] = dist[u] + w
// Check for negative cycle
For each edge (u, v, w):
if dist[u] + w < dist[v]: NEGATIVE CYCLE DETECTED

3.3 Multistage Graph
A multistage graph is a directed graph partitioned into k stages. Edges go only from stage i to stage i+1.
Goal: Find shortest path from source (stage 1) to sink (stage k).
DP Formulation
COST[i][v] = min over all edges (v,w) in stage i+1:
{ c(v,w) + COST[i+1][w] }
// Forward approach (source to sink)
BCOST[v] = min over all edges (u,v):
{ BCOST[u] + c(u,v) }
Dry Run
Graph (4 stages): S→{A,B}, A→{C,D}, B→{C,D}, C→T, D→T

Edge weights: S→A=2, S→B=1, A→C=3, A→D=6, B→C=7, B→D=4, C→T=3, D→T=2
Stage 4 (T): COST[T] = 0
Stage 3: COST[C] = c(C,T)+COST[T] = 3+0 = 3
COST[D] = c(D,T)+COST[T] = 2+0 = 2
Stage 2: COST[A] = min(c(A,C)+COST[C], c(A,D)+COST[D])
= min(3+3, 6+2) = min(6,8) = 6 → via C
COST[B] = min(c(B,C)+COST[C], c(B,D)+COST[D])
= min(7+3, 4+2) = min(10,6) = 6 → via D
Stage 1: COST[S] = min(c(S,A)+COST[A], c(S,B)+COST[B])
= min(2+6, 1+6) = min(8,7) = 7 → via B
Shortest Path: S → B → D → T (cost = 1+4+2 = 7)

Shortest Path: S → B → D → T (cost = 1+4+2 = 7)
Complexity
Time 	O(V + E)
Space 	O(V)
Direction 	Can go forward or backward

3.4 All-Pairs Shortest Paths (Floyd-Warshall)
Finds shortest paths between ALL pairs of vertices. Uses intermediate vertices progressively.
Recurrence
D(k)[i][j] = min( D(k-1)[i][j], D(k-1)[i][k] + D(k-1)[k][j] )
= min( direct path i→j, path through vertex k )
Where k = intermediate vertex (1 to n)
Initialize: D(0)[i][j] = weight(i,j) if edge exists, else ∞; D[i][i] = 0

3.5 Matrix Chain Multiplication
Given n matrices, find the most efficient order to multiply them so that the total number of scalar
multiplications is minimized.
Key Insight
Multiplying an p×q matrix with a q×r matrix costs p×q×r operations. The problem is to place
parentheses optimally.
DP Formulation
m[i][j] = minimum multiplications to compute A_i × ... × A_j
Base case: m[i][i] = 0
Recurrence:
m[i][j] = min over all k (i ≤ k < j):
{ m[i][k] + m[k+1][j] + p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j] }

Space 	O(n²)
Output 	Minimum multiplications + optimal
parenthesization

3.6 Optimal Binary Search Trees (OBST)
Given keys k1<k2<...<kn with search probabilities p[] and dummy key probabilities q[], construct a BST
that minimizes expected search cost.
Formulation
e[i][j] = expected cost of optimal BST for keys k_i ... k_j
w[i][j] = sum of all probabilities in range (weight)
w[i][j] = w[i][j-1] + p[j] + q[j]
e[i][j] = min over all r (i ≤ r ≤ j):
{ e[i][r-1] + e[r+1][j] + w[i][j] }
Base: e[i][i-1] = q[i-1]; w[i][i-1] = q[i-1]
Dry Run

e[3][3] = 0.05+0.10+0.25 = 0.40
Length 2:
e[1][2]: w[1][2]=w[1][1]+p[2]+q[2]=0.45+0.3+0.05=0.80
r=k1: e[1][0]+e[2][2]+0.80 = 0.05+0.60+0.80 = 1.45
r=k2: e[1][1]+e[3][2]+0.80 = 0.60+0.05+0.80 = 1.45
e[1][2] = 1.45 (either root)

3.7 0/1 Knapsack Problem
Given n items, each with weight w[i] and value v[i], and a knapsack of capacity W: select items (each at
most once) to maximize total value without exceeding W.
DP Formulation
dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w
Recurrence:
if w[i] > w: dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w] 	// can't include item i
else: 	dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], // exclude item i
dp[i-1][w-w[i]] + v[i]) // include item i
Base: dp[0][w] = 0 for all w; dp[i][0] = 0 for all i
Dry Run

Backtracking the Solution
Start at dp[n][W]. If dp[i][w] ≠ dp[i-1][w], item i is selected; move to dp[i-1][w-w[i]].
Complexity
Time 	O(n × W)
Space 	O(n × W) or O(W) optimized
Type 	Pseudo-polynomial

3.8 Reliability Design
Given m device types in a series system, and cost/reliability per device, choose the number of devices
of each type (with device replication in parallel) to maximize system reliability subject to a budget
constraint.
Concept
• A system has m stages in series; each stage can have ri copies in parallel.
• Stage reliability: 1 - (1 - φ_i)^r_i
• System reliability: Product of all stage reliabilities.
DP Formulation
f(j, x) = maximum reliability of first j stages with cost x

Best within budget C=10: r=[3,2,4]: check cost & maximize

3.9 Traveling Salesman Problem (DP — Held-Karp)
Find the shortest Hamiltonian cycle — a tour visiting every city exactly once and returning to start. DP
with bitmask reduces brute-force O(n!) to O(n² × 2ⁿ).
DP Formulation (Held-Karp)
dp[S][i] = minimum cost to reach city i, having visited exactly
the set S of cities (starting from city 0)
Base: dp[{0}][0] = 0
Recurrence:
dp[S][i] = min over all j in S (j ≠ i):
{ dp[S - {i}][j] + dist[j][i] }

via 1: dp[{0,1,3}][1]+dist[1][3] ...
Final answer: dp[all][i]+dist[i][0] for all i, take minimum
Optimal tour: 0→1→3→2→0 Cost = 10+25+30+15 = 80
Complexity
Time 	O(n² × 2ⁿ)
Space 	O(n × 2ⁿ)
vs Brute Force 	O(n!) reduced significantly

UNIT IV: BACKTRACKING & BRANCH AND BOUND
PART A: BACKTRACKING
4.1 The General Method
Backtracking is a systematic way to iterate through all possible configurations of a search space. It
builds candidates incrementally and abandons (backtracks) a candidate as soon as it determines the
candidate cannot lead to a valid solution.
State Space Tree
• Each node represents a partial solution.
• Root = empty solution; leaves = complete solutions or dead ends.

• Pruning: Branches that violate constraints are cut off early.
Backtrack(state):
if isGoal(state): record/return solution
for each choice c in generateCandidates(state):
if isPromising(state + c): // bounding function
apply choice c
Backtrack(state + c)
undo choice c 	// BACKTRACK
Key Concept: Backtracking = DFS on state-space tree with pruning. The
bounding/promising function is what makes it efficient.
4.2 The 8-Queens Problem

4.2 The 8-Queens Problem
Place 8 queens on an 8×8 chessboard such that no two queens threaten each other (no two queens in
the same row, column, or diagonal).
Constraint Checks
Place queens one per row. For queen in row r, column c:
1. No other queen in column c
2. No other queen on diagonal: |r1-r2| ≠ |c1-c2|
IsPromising(row, col):
for i = 1 to row-1:
if col == placed[i] 	// same column
or |row - i| == |col - placed[i]| // diagonal
return false
return true

4.3 Graph Coloring
Assign colors to vertices of a graph such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color, using at
most m colors. Find if it's possible (m-colorability) and find all colorings.
Algorithm
GraphColor(v, colors[]): // v = current vertex (1 to n)
for each color c in 1..m:
if isPromising(v, c):
colors[v] = c
if v == n: print solution
else: GraphColor(v+1, colors)
isPromising(v, c):
for each neighbor u of v:
if colors[u] == c: return false
return true

4.4 Hamiltonian Cycles
A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex of a graph exactly once and returns to the starting vertex.
Finding if one exists is NP-Complete.
Algorithm
Hamiltonian(path[], pos):
if pos == n: // all vertices added
if edge exists from path[pos-1] to path[0]: FOUND
else: return false
for each vertex v not in path:
if isPromising(v, path, pos): // edge from path[pos-1] to v?
path[pos] = v
if Hamiltonian(path, pos+1): return true
path[pos] = -1 // backtrack
return false

return false

4.5 Knapsack Problem — Backtracking
Unlike DP (0/1 Knapsack), backtracking explores the state space tree and uses a bounding function to
prune branches.
Bounding Function
Compute upper bound: take fractional part of next item
bound = current_value + (remaining_capacity / w[k]) * v[k]
// Greedy upper estimate using fractional knapsack
If bound ≤ best_so_far: PRUNE (don't explore this branch)

PART B: BRANCH AND BOUND
4.6 Branch and Bound — General Method
Branch and Bound (B&B) is used for optimization problems. Unlike backtracking (which uses DFS),
B&B uses BFS or Best-First search and a cost bounding function to guide exploration.
Key Differences: Backtracking vs Branch & Bound
Feature 	Backtracking 	Branch & Bound
Goal 	Find any/all feasible solutions 	Find optimal solution
Traversal 	DFS 	BFS / Best-First (LC-BB)
Bounding 	Feasibility check 	Cost bound (upper/lower)

Problems 	Decision problems 	Optimization problems
B&B Framework
1. Start with root node in priority queue (min-heap for minimization)
2. Extract node with best bound
3. Branch: generate children by adding one decision
4. Bound: compute upper/lower bound for each child
5. Prune: if bound ≥ current best (for min), discard
6. Update best if a complete feasible solution found
7. Repeat until queue empty
4.7 Branch and Bound — 0/1 Knapsack

4.7 Branch and Bound — 0/1 Knapsack
Use upper bound = current profit + fractional profit of remaining items (like fractional knapsack).
Maximize profit.
Upper Bound Calculation
upperBound(node):
bound = node.profit
remaining_cap = node.weight
j = next item after node.level
while j ≤ n and remaining_cap + w[j] ≤ W:
bound += v[j]; remaining_cap += w[j]; j++
// fractional part of next item
if j ≤ n:
bound += (W - remaining_cap) * (v[j]/w[j])
return bound

4.8 Branch and Bound — Traveling Salesperson Problem
Find the minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle. B&B uses a lower bound based on reduced cost matrix.
Cost Matrix Reduction
Row Reduction: subtract minimum of each row from all elements in that row
Col Reduction: subtract minimum of each col from all elements in that col
Lower Bound = sum of all row-min + sum of all col-min
For each edge (i,j) added to tour:
Set row i and col j to ∞, set path[j][source] = ∞

Set row i and col j to ∞, set path[j][source] = ∞
Reduce new matrix → new LB = parent LB + reduction cost + cost(i,j)

Row B: subtract 4 → [11,∞,12,0]

UNIT V: NP-HARD AND NP-COMPLETENESS
5.1 Basic Concepts
Complexity Classes
Class 	Definition
P 	Problems solvable in polynomial time O(nᵏ)
NP 	Problems verifiable in polynomial time
(Non-deterministic Polynomial)
NP-Hard 	At least as hard as hardest problems in NP (not
necessarily in NP)
NP-Complete 	In NP AND NP-Hard (hardest problems in NP)
The Million Dollar Question: Is P = NP? If any NP-Complete problem has a polynomial
solution, all do. Currently unresolved.
Key Relationships

Key Relationships
P ⊆ NP ⊆ NP-Hard
NP-Complete = NP ∩ NP-Hard
If problem X is NP-Complete:
- X ∈ NP (can verify solution in polynomial time)
- Every problem in NP reduces to X in polynomial time
Polynomial Reduction (≤p)
Problem A reduces to Problem B (A ≤p B) if: given a polynomial-time solver for B, we can solve A in
polynomial time. This means B is at least as hard as A.
Proving NP-Completeness
51. Step 1: Show problem ∈ NP (verify solution in poly time).

52. Step 2: Reduce a known NP-Complete problem to your problem in polynomial time.
First NP-Complete Problem: SAT (Boolean Satisfiability) — proven by Cook's Theorem,
1971. All NP-Complete proofs trace back to SAT.
NP-Complete Problem Chain
SAT → 3-SAT → Clique → Independent Set → Vertex Cover
→ Hamiltonian Cycle → TSP

→ Graph Coloring

5.2 NP-Hard Graph Problems
5.2.1 Clique Decision Problem
A clique in an undirected graph is a subset of vertices where every pair is connected by an edge. The
Clique Decision Problem asks: Does G contain a clique of size k?
Why NP?
• Verification: Given a subset S of k vertices, check all C(k,2) pairs in O(k²) — polynomial.
• Decision: Finding if clique of size k exists is NP-Complete.
NP-Completeness Proof Sketch
Reduce 3-SAT → Clique:
Given 3-CNF formula with k clauses:

Given 3-CNF formula with k clauses:
1. For each literal in each clause, create a vertex
2. Connect vertices from DIFFERENT clauses unless they are
negations of each other (e.g., x and ¬x are NOT connected)
3. Formula is satisfiable ⟺ graph has a clique of size k
This is a polynomial transformation, proving Clique is NP-Hard.
Example
Formula: (x₁ ∨ ¬x₂ ∨ x₃) ∧ (¬x₁ ∨ x₂ ∨ x₄) ∧ (x₁ ∨ x₂ ∨ ¬x₃)
k=3 clauses → need clique of size 3. Select one literal from each clause such that no selected pair is

complementary.
Solution: x₁ from clause 1, x₂ from clause 2, x₁ from clause 3 → satisfying assignment exists.

5.2.2 Node Cover (Vertex Cover) Decision Problem
A vertex cover of a graph G is a set S of vertices such that every edge in G has at least one endpoint in
S. Decision: Does G have a vertex cover of size ≤ k?
Key Relationship
Complement Property: S is a vertex cover of G ⟺ V-S is an independent set of G. Also: Minimum
Vertex Cover + Maximum Independent Set = |V|.
NP-Completeness Proof
Reduce Clique → Vertex Cover (via complement graph):
1. Given graph G and clique size k

1. Given graph G and clique size k
2. Construct complement graph Ḡ (edges where G has none and vice versa)
3. G has a clique of size k ⟺ Ḡ has a vertex cover of size n-k
This is a polynomial reduction → Vertex Cover is NP-Hard
Vertex Cover ∈ NP (verify: check all edges covered in poly time)
Therefore, Vertex Cover is NP-Complete
2-Approximation Algorithm
While uncovered edge (u,v) exists:
Add both u and v to cover
Remove all edges incident to u or v

Remove all edges incident to u or v
This gives ≤ 2× optimal solution size in O(V+E) time

5.3 NP-Hard Scheduling Problems
5.3.1 Scheduling on Identical Processors
Given n jobs with processing times p₁, p₂, ..., p� and m identical machines (processors), assign jobs to
machines to minimize the makespan (maximum completion time).
Problem Formulation
Minimize: Cmax = max(load on any machine)
where load[k] = sum of p[i] for all jobs i on machine k
Optimal Lower Bound: LB = max(max(p[i]), ceil(Σp[i]/m))
This problem (even for m=2) is NP-Hard via reduction from Partition:

Partition: Given S={a1..an}, can we split into two equal-sum subsets?
Reduce to 2-machine scheduling: equal partition ⟺ Cmax = Σai/2
Approximation: List Scheduling (LPT)
LPT (Longest Processing Time first):
1. Sort jobs in decreasing order of processing time
2. Assign each job to the machine with the current minimum load
Approximation ratio: LPT ≤ (4/3 - 1/(3m)) × OPT
Dry Run — LPT with 3 machines, 6 jobs
Jobs: p = [6, 5, 5, 4, 4, 3] (already sorted desc). Machines: M1, M2, M3

Job 1 (p=6): assign M1. Loads: [6, 0, 0]
Job 2 (p=5): assign M2. Loads: [6, 5, 0]
Job 3 (p=5): assign M3. Loads: [6, 5, 5]
Job 4 (p=4): assign M2 (min=5). Loads: [6, 9, 5]
Job 5 (p=4): assign M3 (min=5). Loads: [6, 9, 9]
Job 6 (p=3): assign M1 (min=6). Loads: [9, 9, 9]
Makespan = 9 (optimal since Σ=27, 27/3=9)

5.4 NP-Hard Code Scheduling — Code Generation with Common
Subexpressions
This involves generating optimal machine code with register allocation, especially when expressions
share common subexpressions. The goal is to minimize the number of instructions or registers used.
Core Problem
• DAG representation: An expression can be represented as a Directed Acyclic Graph where
shared nodes are common subexpressions (CSE).

shared nodes are common subexpressions (CSE).
• Register allocation: Determine order to evaluate DAG nodes to minimize register spills
(storing/loading from memory).
• NP-Hardness: Optimal code generation from a DAG (with limited registers) is NP-Hard.
Example: Expression DAG
Expression: (a+b) * c + (a+b) * d
DAG: 	* 	*
/ \ 	/ \
(a+b) c (a+b) d
\ 	/
(a+b) 	← shared CSE
Without CSE recognition: compute (a+b) twice → wasteful
With CSE: compute (a+b) once, store in register, reuse

Optimal code (2 registers):
R1 = a + b 	(compute CSE once)
R2 = R1 * c 	(first multiply)
R1 = R1 * d 	(reuse R1 for second multiply)
R1 = R2 + R1 	(final addition)
Sethi-Ullman Algorithm
Assigns labels (register requirements) to expression tree nodes to minimize register usage.
Label(node):
if node is leaf:
return 1 if first occurrence, else 0
if left.label == right.label:
return left.label + 1
else:
return max(left.label, right.label)

else:
return max(left.label, right.label)
Code generation uses this labeling to choose evaluation order
so that the child requiring more registers is evaluated first.
NP-Hardness Connection
General code scheduling (with branches, shared subexpressions, and limited registers) is NP-Hard.
This is related to:

• Graph coloring for register allocation (chromatic number problem)
• Optimal DAG evaluation order with k registers
